analysis.one_liner: Speeds up federal permits for energy and mining projects and forces approval of one stalled natural gas pipeline.
analysis.headline: Introduced in May 2023 and referred to the Senate Energy Committee the same day, the bill never received a vote or a single cosponsor and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put strict time limits on federal environmental reviews of major energy and mining projects: two years for the deepest reviews, one year for lighter ones, and 150 days for the remaining permits afterward. It would let project developers sue agencies that miss the deadlines, cap public comment periods at 45 to 60 days, cut the length of environmental studies, and shrink the window for lawsuits against approved projects to 150 days. It would also direct federal agencies to reissue every approval for the Mountain Valley Pipeline within 30 days, substantially in the form of earlier approvals, and shield the project from further administrative or judicial delay.
analysis.who_benefits: Energy and mining project developers gain enforceable permitting deadlines they can sue over, priority designations for a guaranteed list of at least 25 projects, and a much shorter window for opponents to challenge approvals in court. The owner of the Mountain Valley Pipeline gains a congressionally mandated finish to a project whose permits had been tied up for years. Utilities and transmission developers gain a federal backstop that can approve interstate transmission lines when states fail to act within a year, and hydrogen pipelines would come under federal permitting authority.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a two-year deadline for the environmental impact statement on a major project, a one-year deadline for lighter assessments, and requires any remaining construction authorization within 150 days of the review's completion.
Lets project sponsors go to court to force agencies that miss the deadlines to act, with expedited court schedules and, generally, a 90-day order for the agency to comply.
Expands the existing FAST-41 fast-track program to cover critical mineral projects and any energy project requiring more than $50 million in investment.

Requires the President to keep a rolling list of at least 25 high-priority energy projects—reserved slots include six fossil fuel projects, five critical minerals projects, seven without fossil fuels, three transmission projects, two carbon capture projects, and two hydrogen projects—and directs agencies to prioritize their permits, backed by $250 million for agency reviews.

Authorizes the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to approve interstate electric transmission facilities when a state fails to act on an application within a year, denies it, or conditions it in ways that defeat the project, and redefines natural gas under the Natural Gas Act to include hydrogen so hydrogen pipelines can be federally permitted.

Requires federal agencies, within 30 days of enactment, to reissue the biological opinion, rights-of-way, forest plan amendment, water permits, and pipeline certificate needed to complete the Mountain Valley Pipeline, substantially in the form of earlier approvals, and states the purpose is to complete the project 'without further administrative or judicial delay or impediment.'

analysis.who_pays: People who live along pipeline, mine, and transmission routes, and the public generally, would get shorter windows to weigh in (comment periods capped at 45 to 60 days), shorter and thinner environmental documents (150 pages in most cases), and only 150 days to sue over an approved project. Communities along the Mountain Valley Pipeline route would lose the ability to challenge its approvals in court at all. Taxpayers would fund $250 million of extra agency review capacity.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near projects and the public

drawbacks.text: Cuts the window for filing a lawsuit over an approved project to 150 days, sends such cases to expedited dockets, and caps court-ordered agency rework on remand at 180 days, sharply limiting the public's ability to challenge a project it believes was approved unlawfully.

Caps the text of most environmental impact statements at 150 pages (300 for unusually complex projects) and caps public comment on a draft statement at 60 days and other comment periods at 45 days, reducing the depth and openness of the review the public sees.

The Mountain Valley Pipeline provision directs agencies to reissue approvals within 30 days substantially in the form of earlier approvals and declares the project should proceed without further judicial delay, removing the court recourse that had repeatedly overturned the pipeline's permits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Permitting delay is a real problem: clean energy, transmission, and even agency capacity suffer when reviews drag on, and some of this bill's coordination and staffing provisions would genuinely help. But the bill's strongest tools—court-enforceable deadlines for developers, page and comment limits, a 150-day lawsuit window, and a bespoke mandate to finish one pipeline over court objections—all run in one direction: away from the communities and public reviewers and toward the companies building the projects. An honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill trades the public's ability to hear about, comment on, and challenge projects for speed, and that its centerpiece is a single pipeline rather than a system fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Manchin introduced the bill on May 2, 2023, and it was read twice and referred the same day to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the Senate.
No committee markup, floor action, or vote ever followed; the referral was the last entry in the bill's action history.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without the bill ever reaching the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee without a vote, communities along the Mountain Valley Pipeline route and other project sites kept full rights to comment on and sue over federal approvals, and agencies kept authority over their own review timelines. Energy and mining developers did not get the shortened deadlines, priority project list, or narrowed lawsuits the bill offered them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities that kept their day in court

for.name: Sen. Joe Manchin III
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia and chair of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 2, 2023; it was his sole sponsorship and no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the bill's own sponsor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on May 2, 2023 and took no further action—no markup, no vote, no report—for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Opponents of the Mountain Valley Pipeline, including environmental groups and residents along the route
against.role: Project opposites whose court challenges the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Sued over and repeatedly overturned the pipeline's federal approvals in court, the recourse the bill's Section 203 sought to eliminate.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a cosponsor from either party and never came to a vote, so no partisan split ever registered; it died in the Energy Committee, whose chair was its own sponsor.

industries.industry: Natural gas pipeline developers (including the Mountain Valley Pipeline's owner)
industries.note: Title II orders every federal agency to reissue the pipeline's missing approvals within 30 days, substantially in the form of earlier approvals, and to complete the project without further administrative or judicial delay. That rescues a specific project at the direct expense of the communities along its route, who lose their ability to challenge it in court.

The bill adds critical mineral projects to the FAST-41 fast track and reserves five of the 25 priority designations for mineral mining, including at least three new extraction projects. Faster, thinner reviews mean mines near communities face less scrutiny and a 150-day window for opponents to sue.

Six of the 25 presidential priority slots are reserved for projects to produce, process, transport, or store fossil fuels, and all such projects get the two-year review cap, capped comment periods, and the shortened lawsuit window.

A FERC backstop can approve interstate transmission when a state sits on an application for a year, and the bill funds faster agency reviews. Building transmission generally serves consumers through reliability and cheaper power, though the federal backstop overrides state and local siting objections.

industries.industry: Clean energy, hydrogen, and carbon capture developers
industries.note: Seven priority slots go to non-fossil generation and clean equipment, two to carbon capture, two to hydrogen, and hydrogen pipelines come under federal permitting. These developers share the same fast-track benefits as their fossil counterparts, and faster transmission permitting helps them reach customers.
